title: Togo at Tsushima
text:
In 1904 Japan went to war with Russia over Korea and Manchuria. Japan's navy had bottled up the Russian Pacific squadron at Port Arthur. Russia sent its Baltic Fleet, under Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky, on an extraordinary voyage of about eighteen thousand miles around Africa to the Far East. The voyage took more than seven months, and by the time the fleet arrived its crews were exhausted and the ships fouled with growth.

Admiral Togo Heihachiro waited for it with a fleet that had trained, repaired and rested. He placed his ships near the Korea Strait, which Rozhestvensky would probably use to reach Vladivostok. On 27 May 1905 Japanese scouts sighted the Russian fleet in the strait of Tsushima. As battle began, Togo hoisted a signal saying that the rise or fall of the empire depended on this battle and that every man should do his utmost.

Togo turned his battle line across the head of the Russian column, so that his ships could bring their guns to bear while the Russians could not answer fully. His faster ships, with better gunnery, concentrated fire on the leading Russian battleships. Over that afternoon and the following night and day, almost the whole Russian fleet was sunk, captured or interned. Rozhestvensky himself was wounded and captured. Japan lost three torpedo boats.

The battle ended Russia's hopes in the war, and a peace treaty was signed at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in September 1905.
lesson: Readiness and position often matter more than size. Let the other side bear the costs of coming to you, and be fully prepared when it arrives.
source: Official naval histories of the Russo-Japanese War; Richard Hough, The Fleet That Had to Die (1958)
